personality_voice.book_baseline: Book Harry is defined by a cluster of interlocking traits: fierce loyalty, moral stubbornness, a hair-trigger temper when those he loves are threatened, deep guilt about the danger he brings to others, and a persistent defiance of authority when he believes it is wrong. He is self-deprecating about his own intelligence but decisive under pressure. His voice is direct and often blunt — he says 'no' flatly when he objects, storms at Lupin for wanting to abandon Tonks, bellows at Hermione when he hates her advice, shouts 'Lies!' in his bedroom at Rita Skeeter's article. He also has a dry, sardonic wit ('What a surprise,' to Vernon; 'I didn't support Puddlemere United' to Mrs. Weasley). He internalises doubt and grief heavily — the long passages where he lies awake brooding about Dumbledore, Voldemort, the Horcruxes, the deaths of those around him — and his internal monologue shows a character who is frightened, self-questioning, and capable of outright fury at Dumbledore. His speech is often short and curt under stress, longer when he argues or explains. He is also notably flawed: he snaps at Hermione, is cruel to Lupin, obsesses over the Hallows to the neglect of the Horcrux mission.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core traits well: defiance (appearing in the Great Hall to confront Snape; challenging Voldemort face-to-face in the final confrontation), loyalty (rescuing Malfoy from fiendfyre, insisting on warning Arthur Weasley, going to the forest alone), and moral stubbornness (refusing to use the Elder Wand, breaking it). The wit is present in small doses — 'I'm a Gryffindor' to McGonagall; the dry exchange with Aberforth. The temper is present in confrontations with Snape and Voldemort. However, the film systematically strips away the long interior passages of self-doubt, resentment, and obsession. The Hallows obsession — one of the most defining characterisation choices in the second half of the book — is present in the film but compressed into a few exchanges. Harry's furious outburst at Dumbledore on the hillside ('Look what he asked from me, Hermione!') is largely absent; the film replaces this with a calmer, more resolved portrayal. The explosive argument with Lupin is cut from the theatrical release (classified as excluded material), removing a key scene that shows both Harry's moral fierceness and his capacity to be cruel. The self-deprecating humour appears but is thinner. Overall the dominant traits survive but the texture — the fear, the resentment, the obsessive episodes — is thinned.
personality_voice.difference: The film loses the interior landscape of Deathly Hallows Harry: the weeks-long Hallows obsession rendering him passive and irritable; the sustained grief and guilt; the fury at Dumbledore that builds chapter by chapter; the self-criticism after Ron leaves. Speech is preserved in confrontation scenes but the quieter, introspective register is largely gone. The Lupin argument (cut from theatrical release) removes a critical display of his moral anger and his capacity to be hurtful. The 'Good riddance' line at Privet Drive replaces a more nuanced farewell where Harry feels the strangeness of leaving his first home.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The dominant personality traits — courage, loyalty, defiance, moral stubbornness — are all clearly present and consistently portrayed. The voice in dialogue scenes is faithful. The penalty is for systematic compression of the inner life: the Hallows obsession, the sustained anger at Dumbledore, the guilt spirals, the snapping at friends. These are not isolated scenes but a pervasive tonal quality in the second half of the book. The loss of the Lupin argument (excluded material) removes one of the most vivid demonstrations of Harry's temper and moral code. This warrants a moderate penalty but not a severe one because the core is intact.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Harry drives the plot throughout Deathly Hallows as the primary decision-maker and initiator. He decides to go to Godric's Hollow over Hermione's objections; he decides to storm into Voldemort's mind; he insists on the Horcrux mission over the Hallows; he initiates the Ministry infiltration plan; he gives the final instructions to Neville about the snake; he chooses to walk into the forest. He is the one who reads Kreacher's history and chooses to treat the elf with kindness, changing Kreacher's loyalty. He interrogates Ollivander, negotiates with Griphook, questions the Grey Lady, confronts Snape in the Great Hall, confronts Voldemort in the clearing. His decisions structurally control every major sequence.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Harry as the central initiating agent in nearly every major sequence. He decides to go to Godric's Hollow, leads the Ministry infiltration, negotiates with Griphook (now giving the sword in exchange for help, a meaningful choice), questions Ollivander and the Grey Lady, confronts Snape in the Great Hall, and walks to the forest. His final confrontation with Voldemort and the breaking of the Elder Wand are entirely his choices and his actions. Agency is high throughout both films.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Two areas of agency loss are notable. First, the Kreacher arc is heavily compressed: in the film Harry questions Kreacher and sends him to find Mundungus, but the extended scene in which Harry consciously chooses to treat Kreacher with kindness and respect — and the transformation in Kreacher that follows — is reduced to a functional transaction. Harry's moral initiative in this relationship is diminished. Second, several moments where Harry argues for or against a course of action against the other two are compressed — for instance, the sustained argument about whether to pursue Hallows or Horcruxes, where Harry's obsession is an active narrative force, is shortened. The Lupin confrontation (excluded theatrical material) would have shown Harry's agency in a morally complex situation; its absence means one instance of him initiating a painful but principled confrontation is lost. Overall, however, Harry remains the undisputed structural driver.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Agency is largely preserved. The compressions reduce texture but do not transfer major decisions or narrative functions to other characters. Harry still decides, confronts, chooses, and acts in every major sequence. A small penalty is warranted for the Kreacher arc diminishment and the Hallows-obsession compression, which together slightly reduce the degree to which Harry's choices are shown to be morally considered and actively wrested from competing pressures.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Harry's motivations in Deathly Hallows operate on multiple levels simultaneously. His primary stated motivation is to destroy Horcruxes and kill Voldemort — fulfilling Dumbledore's mission. But beneath this runs: guilt about the deaths caused by his existence; grief for Dumbledore, Sirius, Hedwig, Mad-Eye; love for his friends and the Weasley family; a deep need to understand Dumbledore (driving the Godric's Hollow visit partly against mission logic); anger and resentment toward Dumbledore for not being honest; and an obsessive desire for the Resurrection Stone rooted in longing for his dead parents. The internal conflict between Horcruxes and Hallows is a sustained psychological drama — not just a tactical debate — revealing Harry's longing for connection with the dead and his difficulty accepting Dumbledore's opacity. His motivation to walk into the forest is explicitly self-sacrifice, driven by love and duty but accompanied by terror.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film accurately captures the primary motivation (destroy Horcruxes, kill Voldemort) and the secondary motivation of loyalty to friends and the Weasley family. The Godric's Hollow visit is framed partly in terms of connection to his parents ('this is where I was born; I'm not returning as someone else'). The Hallows-versus-Horcruxes conflict is present. The self-sacrifice walk is rendered faithfully. The motivation to question Dumbledore — shown in the Bathilda scene, the hilltop argument, and the King's Cross conversation — is preserved in compressed form. The film does not hide that Harry is angry and confused about Dumbledore.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The depth of the Hallows obsession as a motivated psychological state — Harry becoming almost irrational, neglecting mission planning, isolating from Ron and Hermione — is compressed in the film. The specific motivation of longing for the Resurrection Stone to see his parents is named explicitly in the book but only glancingly in the film (choosing the Stone in the 'which Hallow would you choose?' conversation). The sustained internal conflict between trusting Dumbledore and resenting him is reduced from weeks of anguish to a few scenes. The motivational layers are present but thinned.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivations are correctly represented. The internal conflict between Horcruxes and Hallows, between trusting Dumbledore and doubting him, is present. The penalty is for thinning: the Hallows obsession does not register as a fully developed motivational state in the film the way it does across many chapters of the book, and the specific grief-driven desire to use the Stone is underplayed. These are simplifications, not substitutions.

character_arc.book_baseline: Harry's arc in Deathly Hallows moves from a relatively passive boy acting on others' plans (Dumbledore's instructions, the Order's protection) through a period of genuine crisis — loss of Ron, loss of wand, failure at Godric's Hollow, Hallows obsession, growing resentment of Dumbledore — to an earned, active acceptance of self-sacrifice. The arc is not linear: Harry regresses into obsession before recovering. The key turning points are Dobby's death (which shocks him back to purpose); the Pensieve memories of Snape (which reframe Dumbledore's plan and confirm the necessity of his own death); the walk into the forest (the climax of the arc, where Harry chooses death freely); and survival/King's Cross (where he chooses life). By the epilogue, Harry is settled into ordinary life. The arc is about moving from dependence on Dumbledore's plan to autonomous moral choice.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the major arc beats: the crisis of Ron's departure and the Godric's Hollow failure; the recovery triggered by Ron's return and Dobby's death; the Pensieve sequence revealing Snape's memories and Harry's role as a Horcrux; the walk into the forest; King's Cross; survival and final confrontation. The epilogue is present. The arc's shape is recognisable and faithful in its broad strokes.
character_arc.difference: The regression phase — the weeks of Hallows obsession and narrative passivity that constitute a genuine character low point — is compressed into a few scenes rather than a sustained portion of the film. As a result, the arc's central valley is shallower, and the recovery at Dobby's death feels less earned. The specific turning point of Harry consciously choosing the Horcrux mission over the Hallows — a major arc beat where he rejects the Hallows obsession — is present but brief. The arc reads as more linear and heroic in the film than the troubled, regressive, crisis-ridden journey in the book. The epilogue is included, which completes the arc satisfactorily.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The major arc steps are all present and in correct sequence. The penalty is for compression of the low point, which diminishes the arc's emotional weight without eliminating it. The key turning points (Dobby's death, Pensieve, forest walk, King's Cross) are all faithfully rendered. This is a compressed-but-recognisable arc rather than an altered one.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Harry's most important relationships in Deathly Hallows are: (1) Ron and Hermione — the trio dynamic is central, involving genuine tension (Ron's departure, the argument, Harry and Hermione's dance, Harry's guilt about Hermione's suffering), deep mutual dependence, and the specific emotional beat of Harry reassuring Ron about his feelings for Hermione; (2) Dumbledore — a posthumous relationship of trust, growing resentment, and eventual reconciliation, mediated by the Snape memories and King's Cross; (3) Ginny — a love relationship that Harry sacrifices for her protection, thinking of her at key moments; (4) Snape — revealed as a crucial ally whose sacrifice and love for Lily gives Harry crucial information; (5) the Weasley family — Harry's surrogate family, whose losses (Fred, George's ear) wound Harry personally.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The trio dynamic is preserved including the argument, Ron's departure and return, and the dance scene. The Dumbledore relationship is handled through the Snape Pensieve and King's Cross. The Snape revelation is faithful and emotionally effective. Ginny is present and the relationship is indicated, though the private birthday scene (excluded theatrical material) was cut, reducing the most intimate moment between them. The Weasley family grief over Fred is shown. Harry's guilt about the deaths is present.
key_relationships.difference: The Ginny relationship loses significant texture: the birthday scene (excluded material) was cut, as was the moment Harry thinks of Ginny at the wedding and at the forest. The film shows them together but their private emotional connection is thinner than in the book, where Harry's thoughts of Ginny recur as a source of motivation and grief throughout. The Kreacher relationship — where Harry's changed behaviour fundamentally transforms the elf and produces important narrative results — is present but the emotional dynamic (Harry's deliberate kindness, Kreacher's loyalty shift) is compressed into a transaction. The Dumbledore relationship and the Snape relationship are both well-handled.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The most important relationships — trio, Dumbledore/Snape, Weasley family — are functionally preserved. The Ginny relationship is recognisable but thinner. The Kreacher relationship loses emotional depth. These are moderate compressions rather than fundamental distortions of the emotional dynamics. No relationship is reversed or transferred to another character.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book Harry is notably complex in Deathly Hallows: he is a flawed leader who loses confidence and productivity for weeks; he obsesses over objects of questionable value; he is cruel to Lupin in a way that shocks even himself; he snaps at Hermione repeatedly; he lies to Griphook (the sword promise); he uses the Imperius Curse without evident hesitation; he feels bitterness and resentment toward Dumbledore that is never fully resolved before King's Cross. These contradictions — hero who deceives, leader who drifts, moral figure who uses Unforgivable Curses — give the character genuine moral texture. The 'I've done what I can' quality of his final walk into the forest, accompanied by terror and grief, is bookended by weeks of failure and doubt that make it meaningful.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains: the Imperius Curse usage (explicitly shown at Gringotts with Harry noting he's using it for the first time); the sword promise to Griphook which Harry intends to honour vaguely; Harry's grief; the Dumbledore resentment (the hilltop exchange with Hermione); and Harry's willingness to sacrifice himself. The Lupin confrontation (theatrical cut) removes the most striking demonstration of Harry's capacity to be cruel under pressure. The Hallows obsession that makes Harry a poor friend for weeks is compressed, removing the texture of his flawed leadership. The moral complexity of using dark magic is present but not dwelt upon.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Key lost material: (1) The Lupin confrontation (theatrical cut) — Harry's most morally complex interpersonal act in the book, where he calls Lupin a coward and regrets it immediately; (2) The sustained Hallows obsession rendering Harry irritable, uncommunicative, and a worse leader and friend — this is the most significant loss of complexity because it shows Harry as genuinely and temporarily morally compromised; (3) The Petunia farewell (theatrical cut) — a moment of unexpected emotional complexity for Harry; (4) The Dudley farewell (theatrical cut) — where Harry receives unexpected kindness and is moved by it; (5) Harry's extended meditation on Dumbledore's failures and his own resentment; (6) The moral texture of the Kreacher arc (Harry choosing kindness as a deliberate act). Together these removals flatten Harry from a character in sustained moral and psychological crisis to one who is troubled but fundamentally on course.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film Harry is recognisable and retains important complexity — the Imperius Curse, the sword deception, the Dumbledore anger, the self-sacrifice. But the most sustained nuances of the book — the obsession arc, the Lupin cruelty, the Kreacher moral choice — are either cut or compressed to the point where they no longer register as characterisation-building. This is a meaningful simplification of a notably complex portrayal. Cap 1 (above 85 requires preserving major complexity) applies: enough complexity is removed to prevent a score in that range. The total warrants a score reflecting generally faithful but notably simplified character work.

lost_or_transferred_material: Harry's sustained Hallows obsession over multiple weeks — rendered as a temporary fixation rather than a prolonged psychological state that compromises his leadership and relationships
The confrontation with Lupin (theatrical cut) — Harry calling Lupin a coward, then immediately feeling remorse; one of the book's most vivid displays of his temper and moral code
Harry's extended internal fury at Dumbledore across multiple chapters — present in the film but compressed to a single scene rather than a weeks-long resentment
The Petunia farewell (theatrical cut) — Harry observing Petunia's grief and her unspoken acknowledgement of their shared loss
The Dudley farewell (theatrical cut) — Dudley's unexpected declaration that Harry is not 'a waste of space' and Harry's being moved by it
Harry's deliberate kindness to Kreacher as a moral choice that transforms Kreacher's loyalty — reduced to a functional transaction
The private birthday scene with Ginny (theatrical cut) — the most intimate moment between them in the film adaptation
Ron warning Harry and Hermione about the Taboo on Voldemort's name (theatrical cut)
Harry's specific grief-driven motivation for wanting the Resurrection Stone — to see his parents — underplayed relative to the book
Harry's terror and self-doubt during the forest walk, established over weeks of failure in the book, is present in the film but less earned due to the compressed low-point
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 applied: Film removes a significant portion of Harry's complexity (Hallows obsession arc, Lupin confrontation, Kreacher moral arc, sustained Dumbledore resentment), preventing a score above 85 even though remaining material is largely faithful.
key_observations: The film adaptation of Harry Potter in Deathly Hallows is broadly faithful in its most visible dimensions — agency, core personality, arc shape, and key relationships all survive. The dominant traits of courage, loyalty, defiance, and moral stubbornness are consistently present and Daniel Radcliffe's performance reinforces the book's characterisation in confrontation scenes. The primary penalty is for systematic compression of the interior life: the Hallows obsession that consumes Harry for the book's middle section, the moral cruelty of the Lupin scene (theatrically cut), the deliberate kindness to Kreacher as a moral act, and the extended texture of Harry's resentment toward Dumbledore. These losses do not transform the character into someone unrecognisable, but they convert a notably complex, flawed, and psychologically rich portrait into a cleaner heroic journey. The book's Harry is sometimes passive, sometimes wrong, sometimes cruel, and sustained in his doubt for longer than the film permits. The score of 79 reflects a portrayal that is clearly and substantially faithful but has lost enough nuance and moral complexity to prevent placement in the highest tier.
